implementation_notes: TypeScript adds no asynchronous mechanism of its own - the runtime behaviour is JavaScript's promises - but it types the pattern so that its classic mistakes become visible: an async function is declared to return Promise<T>, await produces T rather than a promise, Awaited<T> models the recursive unwrapping that await performs (introduced in TypeScript 4.5), and generic Result/never-typed helpers make the rejection channel explicit where the language leaves it untyped. Promise.all/race/any/allSettled are typed collectors; Promise.all's improved tuple inference predates Awaited<T> (TypeScript 3.9), so the two improvements should not be conflated. Lint rules such as no-floating-promises plus strict null checks turn the pattern's silent-failure anti-pattern into a CI error. The callback realization is modelled as (err: Error | null, value?: T) => void and should be adapted at the boundary with util.promisify rather than nested by hand.
pitfalls: A floating promise with no await and no rejection handler has no error path; TypeScript only flags it with a lint rule, and the rejection is unhandled at runtime.
Promise<T> is erased: a type assertion does not make a decoded JSON payload match T, so results crossing a wire must be validated at the boundary.
Async return types propagate: a helper that forgets Promise<T> in its signature makes callers unwrap incorrectly, and Awaited<T> silently changes when a function stops being async.
await inside a loop serialises calls that could run concurrently - map plus Promise.all is the fan-out form.
Cancellation is carried by AbortSignal, not by the promise type: Promise.race with a timeout leaves the original operation running and, with catch-heavy chains, hides the difference.
